accessibility.text: In our first reading, Hume addresses the question of whether we should believe premises like this by drawing a distinction between two different kinds of claims:
Is the negation of this claim a contradiction?
1. Sample 1 of water froze at 0°C.
2. Sample 2 of water froze at 0°C.
3. Sample 3 of water froze at 0°C.
N. Sample N of water froze at 0°C.
N+1. If all past samples of water froze at 0°C, then \u2028     this sample of water will freeze at 0°C.
C. This sample of water will freeze at 0°C. (1-N+1)
N+1. If all past samples of water froze at 0°C, then this sample of water will freeze at 0°C.
We already have an explanation of why we should believe premises 1-N. What about premise N+1?
It seems as though, if we should believe in the Uniformity of Nature, we should believe N+1. So the basic question is whether we should believe in the Uniformity of Nature.

Premise N+1 appears to be like the claim that the sun will rise tomorrow: it is a matter of fact rather than a matter of the relations of ideas, and so cannot be known “by the mere operation of thought.”
It seems not. So it seems that, if we should believe it, we must believe it on the basis of experience.
Is this argument valid?
The Uniformity of Nature
The future will be like the past.
